analysis.one_liner: Raises the estate tax exemption to $3 million for every estate.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in October 1999 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the amount of an inheritance exempt from the federal estate tax to $3 million per estate, up from the $675,000 level scheduled for 2000 [S2] [S3]. Any estate below that line would have paid no estate tax at all, and the bill would have repealed the separate, complicated deduction for family-owned businesses and farms because it would no longer be needed [S3]. It was introduced by Rep. Dennis Moore, a Kansas Democrat, and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, where it sat without any hearing or vote until the Congress ended [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to estates worth between roughly $675,000 and $3 million would have owed no federal estate tax. Estates above $3 million would have had their first $3 million shielded, cutting their tax bills by hundreds of thousands of dollars. The cut would have taken effect for deaths and gifts after December 31, 1999 [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill raises the unified estate and gift tax credit so that the first $3 million of an estate is exempt from tax, up from $675,000 scheduled for 2000 and 2001 [S2] [S3].

Because every estate under $3 million would owe nothing, the bill also repeals the complex special deduction for family-owned businesses and farms, which existed to protect smaller estates from the tax [S3].
The change applies to estates of people dying, and gifts made, after December 31, 1999 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury would have collected far less estate tax, a cost borne by taxpayers generally. Estate tax revenue comes overwhelmingly from the largest estates, so the foregone revenue would have flowed to the heirs of substantial fortunes.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers, through lost estate tax revenue

drawbacks.text: A $3 million blanket exemption is a tax cut aimed at large inheritances: almost no ordinary estates owe estate tax at the old thresholds, so the benefit would have gone almost entirely to heirs of substantial wealth while shrinking federal revenue [S2] [S3].
Even supporters of estate tax relief faced the tradeoff that revenue lost to blanket exemptions must be made up through other taxes, borrowing, or spending cuts that fall on everyone [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivered one real benefit—shielding family farms and small businesses from estate tax complications with a much simpler, higher exemption—but it did so by granting a full exemption to every estate up to $3 million, which mostly reduces taxes on large inheritances. The tax relief is real, but it is poorly targeted at whoever inherits sizable wealth rather than specifically at family farms and businesses.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so the bill died silently when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Dennis Moore of Kansas introduced the bill on October 21, 1999, with one Democratic cosponsor [S1] [S4] [S5].
The House referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means, the panel that handles tax legislation, on the day of introduction [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever took place, and the bill received no further action before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing happened, so nothing changed: the estate tax remained in place at its existing thresholds, the Treasury kept the revenue it would have lost, and heirs of large estates continued to owe tax as before. Because the bill never advanced, the main party better off is the federal Treasury; the bill's intended beneficiaries, heirs of estates worth up to $3 million, received nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury; large estates still taxed

for.name: Dennis Moore
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise the estate tax exemption to $3 million on October 21, 1999 [S1] [S5].

against.name: Bill Archer
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: The Ways and Means Committee took no action on the bill after its referral—no hearing, no markup, no vote—so it never reached the House floor [S5].

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat introduced the bill and a Democrat cosponsored it [S4], but no vote ever occurred, so no partisan pattern can be measured.

industries.industry: Heirs of large estates and wealthy families
industries.note: The bill would have eliminated estate tax on the first $3 million of every estate, a benefit that flows overwhelmingly to families with substantial wealth. The cost is revenue the Treasury collects mostly from the largest estates, which would otherwise be paid by taxpayers broadly.

industries.industry: Estate planning lawyers and estate-tax life insurance sellers
industries.note: A simpler code with a $3 million exemption would have reduced the need for complex estate planning and for insurance products sold to cover estate tax bills. Some of that complexity exists to benefit families, so its loss is not a pure public gain.
